item.title: Unknotting number is strictly subadditive for the trefoil
item.dc:creator: Anne Dranowski, Yura Kabkov, Daniel Tubbenhauer
item.description:
The computational checks behind the unknotting-number bounds come with a Lean verification, available alongside the authors' data repository.
A trefoil and a certain fourteen-crossing knot take four crossing changes to unknot separately and at most three together. We extend this example to infinitely many prime partners and show that the same partners give a saving for every nontrivial positive braid knot and, up to mirror, every nontrivial torus knot.

item.title: Flag algebras and the exact largest probability of a linear inequality between iid random variables
item.dc:creator: Anton Zaytsev, Pierre C Bellec
item.description:
The exact value of the four-roll supremum (Theorem 1.1), including the probability argument, SDP certificate checks and lower construction, is formalized in Lean 4.
How large can $\mathbb P[X_1+X_2+X_3<2X_4]$ be when $X_1,\dots,X_4$ are independent with a common law $μ$ on $[0,\infty)$? Previous work gave lower bounds through explicit constructions and upper bounds through exchangeability. The best lower bound, $0.4006953723\ldots$, was conjectured by \citet{BF} to be the exact value of the supremum. We prove this conjecture and formalize the proof in Lean 4. The improved upper bound uses the fact that independence gives more than exchangeability: two subsamples are conditionally independent given their shared points. As in Razborov's flag algebras, this yields a semidefinite program on the sign patterns of a few sample points. The new ingredient is to record also whether one sample point exceeds a fixed multiple of another, at ratios read off the extremal construction: with three such cutoffs, four sample points give an exact certificate, while additive comparisons alone leave a gap at seven points. We extend this study to the functions \[ S_2(c) = \sup_μ\mathbb P_μ[X_1+X_2<cX_3],\qquad S_3(c) = \sup_μ\mathbb P_μ[X_1+X_2+X_3<cX_4] \] and determine their exact values on several intervals of $c$. On other intervals, we provide lower and upper bounds that certify eighteen discontinuity points of $S_2$ and five of $S_3$, consistent with a nested staircase structure. The certified jumps are explained by new winning patterns becoming feasible in the lower-bound constructions. We answer Problem 5.3 of \cite{BF} by showing that no coefficient $c$ satisfies $S_3(c)=1/2$, and prove the analogous statement for $S_2$. The thresholds $\sup\{c:S_2(c)\le1/2\}$ and $\sup\{c:S_3(c)\le1/2\}$ are respectively the golden ratio $(1+\sqrt5)/2$ and the silver ratio $1+\sqrt2$.

item.title: Ordering error estimates under mesh-uniform regularity and optimal two-mesh design for the KdV equation with boundary dissipation
item.dc:creator: Kangsheng Liu
item.description:
Theorems 4.1–4.3 (error estimates) were checked in Lean 4 under certain premises; the Lean files are provided as arXiv ancillary files.
We study Galerkin error estimates and optimal two-mesh design for the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation on a bounded interval with boundary dissipation. The ordering error is introduced to measure how much the nonlinearity changes the discretization error. A weighted cubic Hermite Galerkin scheme has mesh-uniform regularity: the discrete semigroups of the linearized equation inherit Crandall-Pazy regularity and Kato smoothing, with bounds uniform in the mesh size $h$. On a small ball of the energy space, the discrete solution maps are also analytic in the initial datum, with bounds uniform in $h$. On this ball the ordering error is at most of order $h^{1/6}$ times the squared energy norm of the datum, for all $t\ge0$. For $u_0$ on this ball and in the domain $D(A)$ of the linearized generator, the bound is of order $h^2\|u_0\|_{H^3}^{3/2}\|u_0\|_{L^2}^{1/2}$. A two-mesh computation adds a nonlinear correction on a coarse mesh to a linear simulation on a fine mesh. Its error is the linear error on the fine mesh plus the ordering error on the coarse mesh. Based on these error estimates, we formulate a model of the optimal two-mesh design: minimize the cost subject to an accuracy constraint given by the error bounds. For data in a small ball of $L^2$, the problem is convex in logarithmic mesh sizes. When the relative error bound for the coarsest allowed mesh exceeds the prescribed tolerance $η$, the optimal pair and its KKT multipliers are unique. For smooth data the problem is convex in the mesh sizes, and the optimal mesh ratio is independent of the tolerance until the coarse mesh reaches its upper limit. In both cases we characterize the small-amplitude limit of the relative cost when the relative tolerance is proportional to the amplitude.

item.title: Undecidable quantum storage: no algorithm can tell from the noise rate whether a fixed circuit remembers
item.dc:creator: Seth Douglas, Nidhal Mghirbi
item.description:
A Lean 4 library with Mathlib, archived on Zenodo, machine-checks selected lemmas, conditional fidelity bounds, lifetime estimates and the certification theorem. The main theorems are not formalized.
Below a threshold noise rate, error correction lets larger quantum memories store a qubit for longer, without limit. Can the noise rate alone tell us whether a given noisy circuit does this? We construct fixed local circuits for which no algorithm can, already in one dimension under single-qubit noise. Each circuit is translation-invariant and time-periodic, with depolarizing noise on every wire after every layer, including all classical control. A computable list of disjoint rate intervals is indexed by the inputs $n$ of a universal Turing machine; local noise statistics select the input that the circuit simulates, and halting triggers erasure. If the machine runs forever on $n$, a qubit is stored throughout the $n$-th interval at entanglement fidelity at least $15/16$ for a time that grows without bound with size: linearly on rings, exponentially in six dimensions. The encoding and decoding maps are noiseless and global; they depend on $n$, the system size and, for decoding, the time, but not on the rate. If it halts, the fidelity of every encoding falls below $1/2+η$, for any fixed $η>0$, after a time independent of size and rate. The labels of the intervals with unbounded storage form a $Π^0_1$-complete set, and intervals of both kinds accumulate at zero, so these circuits have no noise threshold. Without rate selection, the ring construction is a translation-invariant, time-periodic memory: from an initialized classical hierarchy it stores a qubit for a time linear in the ring length at every sufficiently small rate, addressing the memory part of a one-dimensional question raised by Dünnweber, Styliaris and Trivedi. These are existence results: registers and interaction ranges are very large and the rates astronomically small.

item.title: Nilpotent tridiagonal matrices with entries in {-1,0,1}
item.dc:creator: Marcel Blattner
item.description:
Main classification, rigidity theorem, cardinality and modular criterion are formalised in Lean 4 with Mathlib ( 3,000 lines), with a Zenodo artifact.
We determine all nilpotent tridiagonal matrices with entries in $\{-1,0,1\}$. The problem reduces to describing the set $\cN_n$ of pairs $(d,b)\in\{-1,0,1\}^n\times\{-1,1\}^{n-1}$ for which the tridiagonal matrices with diagonal $d$ and with products $b_k$ of opposite off-diagonal entries have characteristic polynomial $λ^n$. We show that $\cN_n$ is obtained from $\cN_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ by one of two explicit “folding” operations, according to the parity of $n$. As a consequence, $\cN_n$ is non-empty precisely when $n=1$ or $3\cdot2^j-1\le n\le2^{j+2}-1$ for some $j\ge0$, in which case it has $2^{\lfloor\log_2n\rfloor}$ elements. This yields a formula for the number of nilpotent $n\times n$ tridiagonal matrices with entries in $\{-1,0,1\}$, which begins $1,9,73,585,4809,39113$. The case $d=0$ is a conjecture of Corless, established in an earlier paper. The main new ingredient is a rigidity phenomenon: a pair as above, of size $n\ge2$, whose characteristic polynomial is congruent to $λ^n$ modulo $4$ is necessarily a fold of a smaller pair. It follows that such a pair is nilpotent as soon as its characteristic polynomial is congruent to $λ^n$ modulo $2^{1+\lfloor\log_2n\rfloor}$. Finally we show that the eigenvalue zero of an $m\times m$ matrix in Corless's skew-symmetric family has multiplicity at most $2^{v_2(m+1)}-1$, with equality attained. The classification, the rigidity statement, the cardinality of the sets $\cN_n$ and the criterion modulo $2^{1+\lfloor\log_2n\rfloor}$ have been formalised in Lean 4.

item.title: Does a Frontier Large Language Model Know What It Can Solve? A 100-Conjecture Calibration Study
item.dc:creator: Ayush Khaitan, Liam Fowl, Tomàs Ortega, Alex Kontorovich, Sanjeev Arora
item.description:
Each of the nine claimed conjecture resolutions comes with a machine-checked Lean 4 certificate built against Mathlib, with axioms audited via #print axioms.
How does confidence correlate with actual performance in large language models, when attacking open research-level math problems? We address this question by studying the performance of ChatGPT 5.6 Sol Ultra on a set of 100 open conjectures in geometric analysis. By construction, the model first selected open problems in geometric analysis that it assessed that it had at least a 50% chance of proving or disproving, and then assigned a probability of success to each question. 13 questions were then excluded after an audit, and the model was asked to resolve the remaining 87 problems. Its mean stated resolution probability was $0.617$, versus an observed rate of $0.103$ (Brier score $0.351$, ECE $0.513$), thereby demonstrating that the model was systematically over-confident in its self-assessment. However, the scores retained ranking signal (AUROC $0.714$). The model was highly overconfident in probability magnitude but did more often than not assign a high probability of success to the problems that it did resolve, than the problems that it did not. Hence, its probabilities were numerically mis-calibrated but directionally correct. All proofs have been formalized in Lean, thereby verifying correctness, and have been run through a semantic equivalence pipeline to ensure semantic equivalence between the formalized and informal statements. These are exploratory campaign outcomes, not fixed-budget success probabilities. The certificates prove formal statements; for a couple of questions, some geometric inputs are assumed in the lean proofs.

item.title: Improving semantic equivalence in research-level math formalization
item.dc:creator: Ayush Khaitan, Liam Fowl, Tomàs Ortega, Alex Kontorovich, Sanjeev Arora
item.description:
Builds a dataset and benchmark of differences between papers and their Lean formalizations, and fine-tunes models to write Lean inside research projects.
Formalizing mathematics in Lean is never a word-for-word translation of a paper: a Lean formalization changes definitions, strengthens hypotheses, splits arguments, and adds lemmas the paper never mentions. It stands to reason that a model that is good at autoformalization must be a good predictor of how a natural language source must differ from its faithful Lean formalization. With that in mind, we collect 4{,}076 audited examples of such changes from 832 Lean projects that formalize research-level mathematics, and use them to ask a practical question: how well can a model write Lean inside a real research-level project that may contain tens of thousands of lines of code, and does training on discrepancies between natural language sources and their faithful Lean formalizations help? Our training set consists of 3{,}431 tasks from 141 repositories, and the test set consists of 645 tasks from the remaining 27 repositories. Training on in-project Lean nearly doubles complete proofs ($11\% \to 20\%$) and raises the share of statements in gold agreement with the project's own formalization by nearly a third ($30\%$ to $39\%$). The gain comes from the pairs themselves: an adapter trained only to predict how the Lean will differ, or a model told the difference in advance, barely helps. Training on where formalizations depart from their sources is thus an effective way of improving semantic equivalence in research-level formalization.

item.title: How many mistakes does it take to learn an interval? Exact Littlestone dimensions of intervals and their unions
item.dc:creator: Miit Daga, Swarna Priya Ramu
item.description:
Exact Littlestone-dimension formulas for intervals and switch-budget classes are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib across 20 files in a public repository.
The Littlestone dimension of a hypothesis class equals the smallest number of mistakes an online learner can guarantee against an adaptive adversary. For discrete intervals and unions of $j$ intervals on $m$ points, only its order of growth was known. We determine it exactly. For every switch budget $k$ (with both end labels fixed when $k$ is odd), the smallest size on which $d$ mistakes can be forced follows a three-regime law: $d+1$ while $d\le k$, then $2d-k+1$, and beyond $d=\lceil 3k/2\rceil+k-1$ doubling the size adds exactly $k$ mistakes. Unions of $j$ intervals on $m$ points correspond to $k=2j$ and size $m+1$, and a single interval gives the thresholds $1,2,3,5,7,10,14,20,\dots$. The natural learner that waits for a positive example and binary-searches both endpoints is not optimal: it can be forced into one extra mistake for 50,847 of the domain sizes below $10^5$. Upper bounds come from a gap potential and a block-pairing learner, and lower bounds from adversary strategies and a refinement step. These tools give an explicit optimal learner with $O(\log m)$ time per round, which on random streams makes more mistakes on average than the natural learner. For randomised learners, we compute the randomised Littlestone dimension of thresholds exactly and prove that a greedy adversary forces an explicit closed-form number of expected mistakes on intervals; this bound is within $0.64$ of optimal and, we conjecture, exact (confirmed for $m\le70$). Exact computation tests every result, and the formulas for every switch budget are machine-checked in Lean 4.

item.title: Praxis: Practical Witness Encryption for NP
item.dc:creator: David Tse, Nikhil Vanjani, Psi Vesely
item.description:
Lean 4 formalization proving correctness and extraction of the Praxis witness encryption scheme at its concrete instantiation parameters, with public repository.
Witness encryption encrypts a message to an NP statement so that whoever holds a witness can decrypt. Over a decade after its introduction, known constructions for general NP statements are far from practical or rest on heuristic or broken assumptions. We propose Praxis, a practical scheme for NP, and prove it extractable in the bilinear generic group and random oracle models under Module-SIS. Our instantiation encrypts to a Groth16 verifier on BN254, set up honestly, which serves every NP relation at the same cost: at $100$-bit security, its ciphertext is $7.88$ GiB, encryption takes $2^{34.2}$ base-field multiplications, and decryption with a Groth16 proof $2^{33.0}$ on average. We give Lean 4 proofs of correctness and extraction at this instantiation's parameters. Praxis starts from the rank-gap template of the recent feasibility result [Hair and Sahai, arXiv 2026]. Where they raise the gap to keep decryption polynomial, we fix it, so decryption ends with a search that is exponential but concretely fast: $O(2^{λ/4} N^{1/4})$ expected operations for a statement in $N$ Boolean unknowns at $λ$-bit security. A quadratic arithmetic program makes our hidden matrix low rank, so where their ciphertext encodes a basis of a matrix space, ours holds factors of width two, which a pairing multiplies. Weights and identities from an extension field tie copies of this matrix, so an adversary telling encryptions apart yields a witness or a Module-SIS solution. For the same Groth16 statement and $100$-bit security level, Praxis reduces the ciphertext size and the cost of encryption of either of their constructions by over ten orders of magnitude, and that of decryption by over six.

item.title: SafeJIT: A Speculating JIT Engine Verified Down to the Machine Code
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Ebner
item.description:
Machine-checked Lean 4 proof, using iris-lean separation logic over Sail ISA models, that the SafeJIT RISC-V and x86-64 binaries never crash.
JIT compilers are among the most attacked components of modern software. They compile attacker-chosen programs, speculate on attacker-influenced type feedback, and run the result at full native privilege. A single wrongly eliminated guard or a missing deoptimization becomes memory corruption. We present SafeJIT, a small JavaScript engine with a speculating baseline JIT, together with a machine-checked proof in Lean 4 that its statically linked RISC-V and x86-64 executables never crash, on any input, in a model of a Linux user process. The theorem is about the shipped binaries, executed instruction by instruction on Sail ISA models (for RISC-V, the official one), and it covers everything in them: the parser and bytecode compiler, the interpreter and its type-feedback recording, the JIT compiler, all machine code the JIT can generate for any program and any feedback (type guards, guard elimination, loop type facts, register allocation with deoptimization metadata, inline caches, deoptimization and on-stack replacement), a mark-sweep garbage collector, the runtime, and a freestanding libc. The C compiler, assembler and linker are not trusted, and neither is floating-point arithmetic. The proof uses separation logic (iris-lean) over a model of a Linux user process whose stuck states are exactly the ways a process can crash, including fetching code that has not been made executable or whose instruction cache has not been flushed.

item.title: Lean Census: A Distributional Analysis of AI-Generated Lean Code
item.dc:creator: Justin Asher, Pietro Pellegrino
item.description:
Measures code statistics of human-written and AI-generated Lean libraries against Mathlib, and releases a Lean analysis package, lean-census.
We compare two human-written and four AI-generated Lean libraries with Mathlib through the distributions of simple statistics of their code. For each library we measure inline claims in proofs, proof length, how often each declaration is used, and design choices such as instances and private declarations, and we read each against the variation among Mathlib's own areas. The AI-generated libraries have more inline claims per theorem, longer proofs, fewer instances, and more private declarations than the human-written ones. We release the code for the analysis as a package, lean-census, at https://github.com/project-numina/lean-census.

item.title: Covering hypercubic grids by polygonal trails: capacity bounds and the optimum for $P(4,3)$
item.dc:creator: Aldo Roberto Pessolano, Marco Ripà
item.description:
Capacity theorem, large-grid lower bound, and boxed construction are verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib; finite exclusions are checked via native_decide reflection.
The classical nine-dot puzzle asks for a polygonal trail through a square grid using as few segments as possible. We study its higher-dimensional analogue on $P(n,k):=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}^k$ for integers $n,k\ge2$, allowing arbitrary real vertices and unrestricted segment directions, and denote the minimum number of segments by $h(n,k)$. For $n\ge3$ and $k\ge2$, we give a geometric proof of the previously stated capacity bound: a trail of $r\ge1$ segments meets at most $1+r(n-1)$ grid points. Refinements of this bound, combined with exhaustive finite checks, establish $h(4,3)=23$ and $h(5,3)\ge32$. We also exhibit a $22$-segment trail through $63$ points of $P(4,3)$, the maximum possible, and a $23$-segment covering trail contained in $[0,4]^3$, which settles the corresponding box-constrained problem. The general capacity theorem, a large-grid lower bound refuting a previously proposed formula for $h(n,k)$, and the boxed construction are verified by the Lean 4 kernel, whereas the finite exclusions use native reflection and additionally trust the native compiler and runtime. A companion technical note provides the computational specification and reproducible proof artifacts.

item.title: Time Series Structure Learning with Local Causal Parent Discovery
item.dc:creator: Jacqueline Maasch, Shu Wan, Hank Zhu, Huan Liu, Zhiguang Wang
item.description:
Soundness and completeness theorems for the ITPD causal discovery algorithm are formalized in Lean 4 core (no Mathlib) via AI-assisted autoformalization, with code released.
Learning and inference on time series can pose significant statistical challenges, including autocorrelated observations, distribution shift over time, and the curse of dimensionality. These challenges complicate the practical application of causal discovery algorithms, which already suffer from high computational and sample complexity in the general case. To mitigate these issues, this work introduces Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (ITPD): a sound and complete constraint-based procedure for causal structure learning on multivariate time series with causal nonstationarity. ITPD takes a local-to-global learning approach that discovers the global graph by sequentially discovering the parent set for each variable. ITPD exploits temporal structural priors, graph partitioning, and the local Markov condition to swap higher-order conditional independence tests for lower-order alternatives. With an exact oracle, ITPD performed the least number of tests and used the smallest average conditioning set sizes relative to baselines. In benchmarking simulations, ITPD sat on the Pareto frontier with respect to F1 and wall-clock time and was faster than baselines on large graphs ($\geq$ 1000 nodes). For graphs with 2000 nodes, ITPD ran $2.3\times$, $9.1\times$, and $40.9\times$ faster than iterative IAMB, DF-PC, and PCMCI, respectively.

item.title: A Model of Diverse Sampling from Language Models
item.dc:creator: Manuel Prada-Corral, Yahya Emara, Timothy J. O'Donnell, Ryan Cotterell, Tim Vieira
item.description:
The KL finite-sample bounds (Theorems 5.1, 5.2, A.4 and Proposition A.2) are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib and released in the code repository.
Language models often produce high-quality individual samples but poor sets, with repeated samples clustering around the same semantic modes. We formalize diverse generation as sampling a size-$K$ subset of complete strings from a determinantal point process (DPP), where the likelihood encodes item quality, and the embedding geometry encodes repulsion between similar outputs. Exact inference over all strings is intractable, so we propose PoolDPP: draw a finite candidate pool from a tractable proposal, importance-weight the candidates toward the target quality, and run a $K$-DPP sampler on the induced pool kernel; a greedy MAP variant provides deterministic selection. We prove a finite-sample bound with an explicit constant: the KL divergence between the sampler's output and the target $K$-DPP decays as O(1/N) in the pool size. Empirically, PoolDPP extends the quality–diversity frontier on open-ended generation and the precision–recall frontier on ambiguous text-to-SQL (Ambrosia), and on mathematical reasoning (GSM8K), it raises diversity at about the same pass@$K$.

item.title: On the $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear relations among multiple zeta values in positive characteristic
item.dc:creator: Jinyuan Hu
item.description:
A Lean 4 formal proof of the paper's results, reportedly generated by ChatGPT, is provided in a GitHub repository.
This paper gives a new path to determine all $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear relations among multiple zeta values in positive characteristic, which had been done by Huang, Lai, Li and the author. The path used in this paper is based on the idea of operator generation, which originated from the work of Todd, developed by the author, and independently by Im-Kim-Ngo Dac.

item.title: Scaling up Multi-Turn Off-Policy RL and Multi-Agent Tree Search for LLM Step-Provers
item.dc:creator: Ran Xin, Zeyu Zheng, Yanchen Nie, Kun Yuan, Xia Xiao
item.description:
Trains an LLM step-prover that generates Lean4 tactics with Lean compiler feedback via LeanDojo, evaluated on miniF2F and ProofNet in Lean.
The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into automated theorem proving has shown immense promise, yet is fundamentally constrained by challenges in scaling up both training-time reinforcement learning (RL) and inference-time compute. This paper introduces BFS-Prover-V2, a system designed to address this dual scaling problem. We present two primary innovations. The first is a novel multi-turn off-policy RL framework for continually improving the performance of LLM step-prover at training time. This framework, inspired by the principles of AlphaZero, utilizes a multi-stage expert iteration pipeline featuring adaptive tactic-level data filtering and periodic retraining to surmount the performance plateaus that typically curtail long-term RL in LLM-based agents. The second innovation is a planner-enhanced multi-agent search architecture that scales reasoning capabilities at inference time. This architecture employs a general reasoning model as a high-level planner to iteratively decompose complex theorems into a sequence of simpler subgoals. This hierarchical approach substantially reduces the search space, enabling a team of parallel prover agents to collaborate efficiently by leveraging a shared proof cache. We demonstrate that this dual approach to scaling yields state-of-the-art results on established formal mathematics benchmarks. BFS-Prover-V2 achieves 95.08% and 41.4% on the MiniF2F and ProofNet test sets respectively. While demonstrated in the domain of formal mathematics, the RL and inference techniques presented in this work are of broader interest and may be applied to other domains requiring long-horizon multi-turn reasoning and complex search.

item.title: APE-Bench: Evaluating Automated Proof Engineering for Formal Math Libraries
item.dc:creator: Huajian Xin, Luming Li, Xiaoran Jin, Jacques Fleuriot, Wenda Li
item.description:
Builds a benchmark of proof-engineering tasks mined from Mathlib4 commit histories, verified by Lean 4 compilation plus an LLM judge.
While frontier formal mathematics systems now routinely develop repository-scale proof engineering artifacts requiring multi-file coordination and semantic correctness beyond compilation, existing evaluation benchmarks remain focused on isolated theorem proving. We introduce Automated Proof Engineering (APE), the first systematic framework for evaluating repository-scale proof engineering through dual verification that validates both syntactic compilation and semantic requirement satisfaction in pinned library environments. We present a complete infrastructure comprising APE-Bench, which automatically extracts proof engineering tasks from real library commit histories, and APE-Harness, a unified execution framework based on task contract abstraction. This contract-based design enables standardized evaluation across diverse formal mathematics tasks and fair systematic comparison of different agent implementations (including our APE-Agent reference scaffold alongside Claude Code and Codex CLI) on identical task specifications. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through comprehensive evaluation. All code and benchmark dataset are released as open-source at https://github.com/xinhjBrant/APE-Bench.

item.title: Exit-Pair Rigidity, Neutral Restart Laws, and Inverse Reconstruction in One Dimension
item.dc:creator: Tony Newton, Juan Antonio Vega Coso
item.description:
Selected results on the exit-pair renewal identities and the discrete analogue are formalized in a Lean 4/Mathlib project (LeanPaperB1), archived on Zenodo.
For an absorbed one-dimensional diffusion, we characterize two-point restart laws preserving the exit-side probability for every independent renewal clock. Spectral identities establish rigidity under spatial accumulation, while explicit nonsymmetric potentials admit neutral pairs. We distinguish midpoint Dirichlet isospectrality from Weyl reflection rigidity and prove a second-order high-energy asymptotic under local continuity, giving two necessary asymmetry conditions for neutral pairs. Two complete exit profiles at distinct reset rates identify diffusivity and drift; a finite birth-death analogue admits exact Jacobi criteria and reconstruction from four channel functions.

item.title: Verifying and Strengthening Neural Tangent Kernel Theory
item.dc:creator: Hao Zhu
item.description:
Formalizes end-to-end NTK lazy-training convergence for two-layer networks in Lean 4 with Mathlib, including matrix Bernstein and gradient-flow existence and uniqueness.
Writing Neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory explains why very wide neural networks trained by gradient methods converge in the lazy-training regime. Its standard proof combines matrix concentration, random Gram matrices, continuous-time dynamics, spectral perturbation, and a bootstrap argument, but has lacked machine-checked verification. We present a Lean\ 4 formalisation for two-layer networks, proving an end-to-end theorem: for a smooth bounded activation (instantiated with $σ=\tanh$), frozen biases, paired $\pm 1$ initialisation, and explicit width conditions, gradient flow exists uniquely with probability at least $1-δ$, and $$ \|r(t)\|^2 \leq \|y\|^2 e^{-λ_0 t/2}. $$ The sole data assumption is population NTK non-degeneracy, $λ_0>0$. Initial coercivity, kernel drift, the movement bootstrap, the residual ODE, and flow existence and uniqueness are formally proved. The formalisation also sharpens the standard analysis in two ways. First, replacing the conventional matrix-Bernstein variance proxy with the classical row-covariance proxy yields estimated concentration-width certificates for $\tanh$ that are $36$–$53\times$ smaller at $(m,d)=(16,8)$ and $94$–$121\times$ smaller at $(32,16)$. Lean certifies the inequality; the ratios are numerical. Second, the network Hessian has operator norm $Θ(\sqrt{p})$ on the sup-norm parameter ball (a paper calculation), preventing the expected $O(1/\sqrt{p})$ linearisation bound via sup-norm Taylor estimates. An $L^2$ parameter geometry resolves this issue. Required widths remain polynomial but far beyond practical scales, limiting applicability.

item.title: Dugong: Composing Uncertified DAG Consensus
item.dc:creator: George Danezis, Lefteris Kokoris-Kogias, Alberto Sonnino
item.description:
Formalizes a parameterized DAG consensus protocol in Lean 4 and Mathlib, proving safety, liveness and composition across about 125,000 lines, with mostly AI-generated proofs.
There is a significant number of uncertified DAG consensus protocols spanning partial synchrony and asynchrony as well as crash, Byzantine, and hybrid fault models, yet each protocol is designed, proved, and implemented from scratch. We introduce Dugong, a single parameterized protocol that unifies uncertified DAG consensus protocols. Its core algorithm, the Decider can implement eight existing protocols and yields four new ones by just tuning its parameters. Given the property that DAGs decouple throughput from latency Dugong presents a simple trade-off between latency and resilience to network and node faults. An operator can adapt the parameters of their protocol epoch-by-epoch to adjust the resilience without needing to develop a new protocol or worry about throughput. Around the Decider, Dugong layers production feature mechanisms (adaptive leader scheduling, checkpoints, responsive liveness, and crash recovery) that provably compose with each other and with the Decider's configurations. We formalize Dugong in Lean 4, proving safety and liveness under the established definitions of Byzantine atomic broadcast, and identify and repair gaps in published proofs. Finally, we implement Dugong as a reusable Rust library paired with a discrete-event network simulator, enabling direct latency comparisons across network and fault models.

item.title: Trotter Error Bounds in Lean 4 with a Cancellation-Aware Analysis of the Fourth-Order Suzuki Formula
item.dc:creator: Bingyu Xia, Jue Xu, Yue Wang
item.description:
Formalizes the Childs et al. commutator-scaling Trotter error bound and fourth-order Suzuki formula estimates in Lean 4 with Mathlib.
We formalize the commutator-scaling bound of Childs et al. in Lean 4. For skew-adjoint generators, the local order condition gives an explicit integer step count sufficient to meet a prescribed error tolerance. We apply the theorem in Lean to the binary fourth-order Suzuki formula. For this formula we can also account for cancellation within and between steps. Using local remainder estimates of Casas and Murua, we sum the signed quintic and centered seventh-degree error terms after conjugating each to the interaction picture. For every positive integer step count, we bound the difference between this sum and the global error operator. At fixed time the explicit remainder is eighth order in the step size, and the integral of the conjugated quintic term gives the exact leading error coefficient. The Lean proofs cover the two-generator finite-sum estimates, including the spectral norm for complex matrices. On five ten-site nearest-neighbor Heisenberg instances at time $10$ and tolerance $10^{-3}$, the transported sum meets the tolerance at a mean of $129.4$ steps. Taking a separate norm at each step with the same polynomial and remainder gives a mean first crossing between $184.6$ and $185.2$ steps. The accumulated Casas–Murua local bound at $q=8$ gives a mean of $184.8$ steps.

item.title: Improved Accuracy Scaling with Problem Complexity in LLM Arithmetic Reasoning Using Executable Symbolic Representations
item.dc:creator: Yu-Bin Liu, Shi-Ju Ran
item.description:
LLMs are fine-tuned to emit executable Lean 4 programs for arithmetic word problems, which are compiled and executed with Lean 4.27.0-rc1 for scoring.
High accuracy on mathematical benchmarks does not establish whether reasoning remains reliable as problem complexity increases. We examine how executable symbolic representations change accuracy scaling in large language models compared with natural-language reasoning. To address this limitation, we introduce the GSM Arithmetic Benchmark (GSM-AB), a controlled benchmark that independently varies operand digit length and operation count to probe numerical scale and compositional complexity. We find that executable representations can improve accuracy and slow its decline as complexity increases. Lean reduces average sensitivity to operand digit length at every tested model size. By contrast, slower degradation with increasing operation count emerges at the larger model sizes. A Python program-of-thought (Python-PoT) control shows a similar operation-axis pattern, suggesting that this finding is not specific to Lean. These findings show that reasoning representation shapes arithmetic accuracy scaling and support executable symbolic representations for more reliable reasoning on complex arithmetic tasks.

item.title: Moonshine Conjecture Formalized
item.dc:creator: Jin-Cheng Guu
item.description:
Formalizes the Moonshine theorem in Lean by connecting the VOA and CFSG repositories, migrating Lean/Mathlib versions and building Griess algebra bridges.
The celebrated and intimidating Moonshine Conjecture has now been formalized in Lean. This achievement might suggest that, once a sufficiently large library compiles, the principal mathematical work is complete. This paper tells a less optimistic story. During our formalization project, we repeatedly encountered two problems that a formally checked proof alone does not settle: (1) whether the formal statements actually express the mathematics we humans expect, and (2) how that meaning survives as the repositories and their dependencies evolve. We argue that there is no magic pill that turns a large agent-produced library into mathematics a community can trust. Even after the proofs are checked by the Lean kernel, someone must judge whether the definitions and statements express the intended mathematics and whether future updates preserve that meaning. This work, even when done, can only be trusted. We must therefore return to the usual trust model: relying on the mathematical judgment of maintainers and expert communities. But semantic review is expensive, making it tempting to keep producing code and take successful kernel checks as sufficient grounds for trust. This shortcut accumulates semantic debt: definitions and results with unchecked mathematical interpretations are reused as foundations for further work. A library may keep compiling and produce the desired formal theorem while users lose track of which mathematical claims they can responsibly rely on. Reliable reuse is also a prerequisite for Terence Tao's vision of formal mathematics as something people can navigate, explain, learn from, and build with. This paper takes our work connecting the VOA and CFSG repositories for the Moonshine Conjecture as a case study of the challenges of reliable reuse as formal developments scale.

item.title: Budget-Aware Predict-and-Verify Theorem Proving with Heterogeneous LLM Solvers
item.dc:creator: Wei Jiang, Ziran Liu, Wei Wang
item.description:
Allocates proof attempts from Lean-targeting LLM provers (Goedel, Kimina, DeepSeek-Prover) over decomposed subgoals; Lean checks the generated proofs, with automation tactics run first.
Large language model (LLM) theorem solvers differ in both proving capability and inference cost. Applying an expensive solver to every subgoal wastes computation when cheaper models are sufficient, while always starting from the cheapest solver wastes attempts on subgoals that require stronger models. We present BudgetPV, an agentic budget-aware predict-and-verify system that allocates computation across unresolved subgoals and heterogeneous LLM solvers. BudgetPV uses a cross-solver predictor to guide solver selection for each subgoal and revises the allocation as verification feedback becomes available. The allocation problem changes as proving progresses. Early decisions mainly determine which solver should handle an untried subgoal, while later decisions determine which previously attempted subgoals should receive additional computation. We train the predictor with two objectives for these two stages. Class-weighted cross-entropy improves assignment to less frequent stronger solvers during the initial stage, while plain cross-entropy provides better calibrated probabilities for later allocation among previously attempted subgoals. We evaluate BudgetPV on Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench using three progressively expanded solver settings: a strong but expensive solver alone, adding a medium-cost solver with intermediate solving capability, and further adding a cheap solver with lower solving capability. BudgetPV requires less LLM generation computation than uniform allocation to solve the same number of subgoals across the evaluated settings. The experiments further show the computation savings obtained as medium- and lower-cost solvers are added.

item.title: The Strong AJ Conjecture for Hyperbolic Prime Knots is False
item.dc:creator: RJ Acuña
item.description:
An AI agent formalized in Lean the mathematical machinery behind the colored Jones function computation, and parts of the counterexample argument.
Let $K$ be a knot in $S^3$. The strong AJ conjecture relates two of its invariants. The first is the minimal-order annihilator $\widehat A$ of the $n$th colored Jones polynomial $J(n)$. The second is the two-variable $A$-polynomial of Cooper, Culler, Gillet, Long, and Shalen. The conjecture says that after specialization $\varepsilon^*(\widehat A)\asymp A$. Zhang gave the first family of composite-knot counterexamples. For $8_{11}$ the specialization of $\widehat A$ carries an extra trefoil factor $L+M^6$. We prove this by verifying Lê's $\widehat P=\widehat A$ conjecture. Zhang's corrected formulation of the AJ conjecture agrees with Lê's weak AJ conjecture, which we prove for $8_{11}$. Li, Li, and Sun have since reported counterexamples of the weak AJ conjecture among non-hyperbolic prime knots. This work was AI assisted, and parts of it have been formalized in Lean.

item.title: Finite-Time Singularity Formation for the Three-Dimensional Euler Equations
item.dc:creator: Levent Alpöge, Tristan Buckmaster, Matei P. Coiculescu
item.description:
The proof of finite-time Euler blow-up is formalized in Lean, with the formalization in a public GitHub repository.
We construct smooth periodic initial data for the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations whose solution blows up in finite time. The velocity remains bounded, while the vorticity magnitude at the origin tends to infinity. Away from the origin, the velocity and its time derivative have smooth spatial limits at the singular time. The construction uses localized Craik–Criminale waves as building blocks of a multi-scale construction.

item.title: A reciprocal-matrix proof of Sendov's theorem and applications to control theory
item.dc:creator: Latchezar P. Tomov
item.description:
The Sendov proof, feedback-law stability bounds, and finite-range integer-arithmetic subdivision checks are formalized in Lean 4, with an interactive proof map.
This proof grew out of the author's research on interpreting mathematical statements from the viewpoint of control theory. Its value lies both in the understanding it brings and in the applications that arise from the argument. Let $a$ be a simple zero of a polynomial of degree $n\ge 2$ whose zeros lie in the closed unit disk. If $c_1,\ldots,c_{n-1}$ are its critical points, counted with multiplicity, then the reciprocals $1/(a-c_j)$ are the eigenvalues of an explicit matrix built from the other zeros. A failure of Sendov's bound at $a$ would therefore make the associated discrete-time system asymptotically stable. This observation leads to an alternative proof of the quadratic inequality of Tang and Zhang, including its equality case. Building on the reflection and centering arguments of Mazur, Tao and Zhang, we estimate the change in the integral of the derivative product when all the reciprocal displacements are replaced by their mean $s$. An exact pairwise cancellation bounds the difference in terms of the variance. For an interior zero rotated to $0<a<1$, the normalized trace $s$ determines a contour through $\overline{s}/a$. If the mean squared reciprocal distance is at most one, integration along this contour gives $(n-1)(2a\Re(s)-a^2)<20$. A uniform phase estimate and reflection at $1/a$ then rule out this possibility in every degree $n\ge 257$. A fourth-moment estimate treats degrees two through five. For degrees five through 256, three bounds derived from one polynomial moment identity exclude the full range of the two remaining real parameters by exact integer arithmetic. As an application, Sendov's theorem illustrates how differentiating the denominator of a closed-loop transfer function can increase robustness in discrete-time systems and decrease it in continuous-time systems. The proofs have been formalized in Lean 4.

item.title: Self-verifiable LLM-driven science and why it needs human researchers
item.dc:creator: Michael G. Medvedev, Nikolai V. Krivoshchapov, Stepan N. Ostarkov
item.description:
An LLM agent formalizes scientific (non-mathematical) arguments in Lean 4, deriving conclusions from human-reviewed assumptions checked by the Lean kernel.
Language models are now used throughout all sciences - for reading literature, extracting numbers from tables and spectra, analyzing data, drafting conclusions - and their answers arrive in the same polished confident tone whether they are right or wrong, so a result has to be re-derived by a human researcher before it can be relied on. The cost of that re-checking, not the ability to generate results, is what currently limits AI-assisted research. In the field of mathematics, this problem is solved by proof assistants like Lean 4 and Coq that let any formal statement and its proof be written down and checked - a perfect match for LLMs, which are now actively used to search for proofs with every step automatically validated, rather than relying on a human to judge the result. In this paper, we propose an extension of this approach to non-mathematical sciences. We describe an AI agent harness that aims to make LLM's scientific reasoning verifiable: the starting assumptions are proposed by LLM and reviewed by a human, and everything built on top of them is checked by a machine with Lean 4. We illustrate how this mechanism works in practice on several examples and our results show that scientific arguments in these tasks can be expressed as formal proofs from explicit assumptions, including experimental results, known theoretical statements, and additional assumptions, produced by the agent. We suggest that this approach could change how scientific research is conducted across all sciences.

item.title: Uniformising random greedy maximal independent sets on graphs with at most five vertices
item.dc:creator: John Fairfax-Ball
item.description:
The full classification of EGU graphs on at most five vertices, including the real exponential-clock law and the P5 obstruction, is formalized in Lean 4.
A random greedy algorithm scans the vertices of a finite graph in increasing order of independent exponential arrival times and accepts each vertex unless an accepted neighbour blocks it. We ask an inverse question: can strictly positive finite arrival rates be chosen so that the terminal inclusion-maximal independent sets are all equally likely? We call this exact property exponential greedy uniformisability (EGU). We establish the complete small-order classification: every finite simple graph on at most five vertices is EGU, with the unique exception of the five-vertex path $P_5$ up to graph isomorphism. A strict $2\times2$ probability minor provides an explicit obstruction for the exceptional graph; the positive cases are certified by graph-isomorphism reduction and exact constructive witnesses. We explain the independent-exponential-clock probability law and the formal Lean 4 verification, registered as Palomar PALOMAR-2026-11-19-000021 (version 1). The registration is a formal proof record, not a claim of novelty certification or journal peer review.

item.title: Whitehead doubles and the failure of the AJ conjecture
item.dc:creator: Jinzheng Li, Yuqi Li, Hao-Yu Sun
item.description:
The failure of the AJ conjecture for Whitehead doubles is formalized in Lean 4, with kernel replay, axiom checks, and independent nanoda and Comparator verification.
For marked Whitehead doubles of torus knots with coprime parameters $2\le r<s$, the AJ conjecture fails for both clasp signs, both companion chiralities, and every integer twist. The zero-framed signed unreduced colored Jones sequence has a nonzero rationally saturated annihilator. Every nonzero primitive representative specializes nontrivially at $t=-1$ with the meridian variable $M$ independent. With $L$ the longitude variable, the specialization contains the irreducible quadratic $E=L^2-(M^4-4M^2+1)L+M^4$ for the negative clasp and $M^4E(M^{-1},L)$ for the positive clasp. The corresponding quadratic is coprime to the full classical $A$-polynomial, including $L-1$, over $\mathbb{Q}(M)[L^{\pm1}]$, so the discrepancy persists when each irreducible factor is counted once. The curve $E=0$ comes from the marked Whitehead link exterior with its axis cusp complete. For the displayed monic polynomial, $πm(E)$ is the unsigned volume of that two-cusped exterior. We use the actual Jones sequence to select a right divisor of the satellite transfer operator. Rational factor tests show that the quadratic survives in this divisor, and the two marked companion fillings exclude it as a component of the satellite boundary curve.

item.title: Stafford's conjecture on cyclicity of torsion modules
item.dc:creator: Christopher Albert, Johanna Moser, Maximilian Philipp
item.description:
Proof of Stafford's conjecture, including Gabber's involutivity theorem and further generalizations, is fully formalized in Lean 4 with archived sources.
We prove that over a Weyl algebra over a field of characteristic zero $A_n(k)$, every nonzero $d\in A_n(k)$ admits $F,R,S\in A_n(k)$ such that $1=dR+FdS$, a conjecture Stafford proposed in 1978. As a consequence, every finitely generated torsion right $A_n(k)$-module is cyclic. The proof maps $d$, by a symplectic change of variables, to a normal form $\tilde d$ and shows that the cyclic module $Q=A_n(k)/(\tilde dA_n(k)+x_1^N\tilde dA_n(k))$ vanishes. We first show that right multiplication by $x_1$ is surjective on $Q$. A comparison of lengths of localized modules over the associated graded ring then gives $\operatorname{gr}Q=x_1\operatorname{gr}Q$, so that the characteristic variety of $Q$ is disjoint from the hyperplane $\{x_1=0\}$. Finally, Gabber's involutivity theorem together with an argument about conormal directions at infinity from algebraic geometry shows that such a characteristic variety must be empty and therefore, $Q = 0$.

item.title: Free Products of Vector Lattices
item.dc:creator: Gonzalo Martínez-Fernández, Pedro Tradacete
item.description:
All numbered results and definitions are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib and a Banach lattice library, each statement linked to its Lean declaration.
We study free products of vector lattices and their relation to free products of Banach lattices. We characterize the Archimedean vector lattices whose vector lattice free product with every Archimedean vector lattice is again Archimedean: these are precisely those whose finitely generated sublattices are projective. For finitely generated lattices, this connects the free-product property with polyhedral geometry through Baker–Beynon duality. We also show that the Banach lattice free product is the completion of the Archimedean vector lattice free product under the largest lattice norm making the canonical maps contractive. For finitely many factors, the Archimedean vector lattice free product is order dense in the Banach lattice free product. Moreover, it is shown that bounded families of injective lattice homomorphisms also induce injective homomorphisms between Banach lattice free products. Finally, in analogy with the theory of separably injective Banach lattices, we study relative injectivity and universal disposition for the class of vector lattices with countably many proper prime ideals. Every vector lattice embeds into one of universal disposition for this class, while ordered ultrapowers of the real line provide relatively injective examples of cardinality continuum.

item.title: Scalable Non-Parametric Bayesian Inference of Free Energy Landscapes and Emission Functions from Observations
item.dc:creator: Eliane Briand, Helmut Grubmüller
item.description:
Partially formalizes the convergence proof of the parallel-in-time filtering algorithm in Lean 4/Mathlib, assuming missing pieces such as Birkhoff contraction and SDE theory as hypotheses.
Free-energy landscapes govern processes from protein conformational change to climate oscillations, but are typically observed only indirectly, through observables such as FRET intensity or optical-tweezer transmittance. Neither the landscape shape, nor the emission function mapping latent state to signal, is usually known, and distinct states may produce the same signal. We therefore infer landscape and emission function jointly and non-parametrically, using the exact non-linear Bayesian filtering likelihood, to fully use the information contained in observable trajectories that are often noisy, scarce and costly to acquire. A novel parallel-in-time algorithm makes this tractable: it is up to 27 times faster than sequential filtering on one GPU, scales near-ideally across GPUs, and, given enough resources, has runtime independent of trajectory length. We demonstrate the method on a single-protein optical tweezer recording, where distinct conformations produce the same signal, and beyond biology on the El Nino-Southern Oscillation and financial market volatility.

item.title: First Order Geometry of Equilateral Small Polygons
item.dc:creator: José Ayala Hoffmann, Tomás Ayala Coppola
item.description:
A Lean 4 formalisation in the ESP1 package verifies the strict local maximality criterion and the maximality results for A16, A32, A64, Z32 and Z64.
We develop a first order calculus based on the geometry of realised diameter graphs for perimeter maximisation among convex equilateral small polygons. Polygon side equalities and active diameter constraints define a linearised feasible cone and an associated equality space. We prove that an equilateral small polygon is a strict local maximiser of perimeter modulo Euclidean motions if a multiplier balance holds with strictly positive active diameter multipliers and the active equality space consists only of infinitesimal Euclidean motions. The proof uses a local Euclidean slice and a geometric limiting argument and requires neither independence of the active constraint gradients nor second order information. As an application, we combine our criterion with validated interval arithmetic to establish strict local maximality for Bingane and Audet's polygons $A_{16}$, $A_{32}$, $A_{64}$ and for reconstructions of their polygons $Z_{32}$ and $Z_{64}$. For each $n\in\{32,64\}$, the perimeter of $Z_n$ is strictly larger than that of $A_n$. Thus, strict local maximisers with different perimeters coexist in the space of convex equilateral small polygons with the same number of sides.

item.title: Convergence of a Parametric Symmetric Galerkin Boundary Element Method for the Mullins-Sekerka Flow
item.dc:creator: Tokuhiro Eto
item.description:
The main convergence theorem and principal auxiliary results are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, archived on Zenodo, and built on a prior Lean formalization.
We prove convergence of the fully discrete parametric scheme for the two-phase Mullins-Sekerka flow of a closed curve in the plane. The scheme combines piecewise linear parametric curves, a curvature discretization of Barrett–Garcke–Nürnberg type and a symmetric Galerkin boundary element approximation of the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map. For a smooth solution whose curves satisfy a capacity condition, a uniform parameter mesh of size $h$, a constant time step $τ$ and exact boundary element integrals, we show that the discrete curves stay regular and embedded, and that their distance to the exact curves in the topology $W^{1,\infty}$, after reparametrization by arclength, tends to zero in the first order of the time-step size $τ$ whenever the mesh size $h$ is bounded by $c_0τ^2$ for some $c_0$.

item.title: Obstructions to Hadamard Deformations of Fourier Matrices
item.dc:creator: Shuler Hopkins, Remus Nicoara
item.description:
The authors state the manuscript's results were formalized in Lean 4 with assistance from ChatGPT Astra; no Lean repository is cited.
We study deformations of the Fourier spin model commuting square in the space of commuting squares, or equivalently deformations of the matrix $\sqrt nF_n$, where $F_n$ denotes the Fourier matrix, by complex Hadamard matrices. If $n$ is neither a prime power nor twice a prime, we show that there exist unit vectors in the enveloping tangent space that cannot be realized as directions of convergence of sequential deformations. Consequently, the derivative of any differentiable Hadamard family through $\sqrt nF_n$ has rank strictly smaller than the dimension of the enveloping tangent space at $\sqrt nF_n$ (i.e., the defect of $F_n$). This is particularly surprising because for every $n$ there exist enough one-parameter analytic families to provide a basis of directions in the enveloping tangent space. We obtain cubic obstructions when $n$ has at least three distinct prime divisors, quartic obstructions when it has exactly two and a repeated factor, and quintic obstructions when it is the product of two distinct odd primes. These results extend our order $30$ result from \cite{HN}.

item.title: Robust Passive Quantum Memory in Three Dimensions, Part I: Thermal and Zero-Temperature Perturbative Stability
item.dc:creator: Patrick Hayden
item.description:
Core stability theorems are stated in Challenge.lean and machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with a repository cross-referenced to the paper's results.
Whether a three-dimensional quantum many-body system with geometrically local, bounded-degree interactions can passively protect encoded quantum information has remained a central open question since Kitaev introduced topological quantum computation. Passive protection requires stability against both thermal noise at nonzero temperature and generic static Hamiltonian perturbations Balasubramanian, Davydova, and Lin (BDL) recently established unperturbed three-dimensional thermal self-correction using a recursively defined family of stabilizer Hamiltonians. However, they left open whether their construction remains stable against quantum perturbations, even at zero temperature. In this paper, we show that a slight variant of the BDL code family achieves stability along both boundary axes of the perturbation-temperature phase diagram as the system size grows. Following BDL, in the absence of perturbation it is thermally stable below a critical temperature, achieving a stretched-exponentially long memory lifetime when coupled to any local Markovian thermal bath generated by single-site system-bath interactions satisfying detailed balance with bounded coupling rates. At zero temperature under arbitrary weak, superpolynomially decaying quantum perturbations, the family maintains a uniform bulk spectral gap, superpolynomially small ground-space splitting, and a superpolynomially long closed-system unitary memory lifetime for quasi-locally dressed logical observables. To prove this zero-temperature stability, we establish local topological quantum order across the multiscale hierarchy using a linearly dilated relaxation of the usual Bravyi-Hastings-Michalakis criteria. In the companion paper, we combine the tools developed here with finite-temperature worldline cluster expansions to establish passive self-correction throughout the phase diagram's positive-temperature perturbed interior.

item.title: FCP: Formal Context Protocol for Verifying LLM-Generated Artifacts
item.dc:creator: Shashank
item.description:
Lean 4 proves the paper's propositions and corollary (84 theorems) and provides a reference semantics checking the FCP-PL-to-monitor compiler registers.
When a language model writes both an artifact and the tests meant to check it, a passing test is weak evidence: one misreading of the request yields a faulty artifact and a check that accepts it. We present the Formal Context Protocol (FCP), which checks AI-generated artifacts against the request itself. FCP separates conformance (does the artifact satisfy a formal reading of a requirement?), which model checkers and SMT solvers decide, from fidelity (does the reading mean what the prose means?), which has no decision procedure but is refutable by a concrete witness. Eight ways a proof can falsely certify a requirement each become a mechanical check that returns a witness, and what no machine can settle becomes concrete questions for the request's author. Adapters place hardware, text, agents and code on the same engines. On four hardware designs, trusting AI-written assertions certified 23% of violated requirements, and FCP certified none. On ten code tasks, code from three language models passed its own tests and violated the request every time. Trusting the tests certified all 33 violations, and FCP certified three. Agreement among models, readings or tests did not imply correctness.

item.title: Counting formulas and refined generating functions for inversion-sequence Classes 152 and 207
item.dc:creator: Haobo Ma, Toufik Mansour, Wenlin Zhang
item.description:
Results are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with pinned versions and a check command given in the supplementary material.
For the two Class 152 pattern sets, we prove that the common number of inversion sequences of length \(n\geq 1\) is \(a_n=1+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\binom{2j}{j}\). The Class 152 proof uses first-descent and last-zero decompositions, with weighted Dyck paths evaluating the resulting generating functions. For Class 207, we prove equality of the three total-count series and give their common generating function as an explicit Lambert-series expression after the substitution \(z=q/(1+q)^2\). Complete legal-site and catalytic recurrences lead to a Lambert series for one class and \(q\)-product orbit sums for another. A cubic limit of the balanced nonterminating \({}_3φ_2\) \(q\)-Saalschutz summation identifies these expressions. Fixed-maximum expansions, finite verification data, refined analytic obstructions, and signed specializations are recorded in the supplementary material.

item.title: Nearly Settling the Complexity of Connected $\varepsilon$-Envy-Free Cake Cutting
item.dc:creator: Simon Mackenzie, Mashbat Suzuki
item.description:
A Lean 4 development using Mathlib verifies the paper's query-complexity theorems (upper bounds for four and five agents, lower bound for seven or more).
Envy-free cake cutting has been one of the central problems in fair division. In cake cutting, agents' preferences over the cake are accessed through Robertson–Webb (RW) queries. For three or more agents, no algorithm that makes finitely many RW queries can always find a contiguous, exactly envy-free allocation. For contiguous $\varepsilon$-envy-free allocations, however, Hollender and Rubinstein (JACM, 2025) showed that $\poly(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ RW queries suffice for four agents, leaving open whether such a bound is possible for five or more agents. In this paper, we establish a striking change in query complexity: $\poly(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ RW queries suffice for up to five agents, whereas $(1/\varepsilon)^{Ω(1)}$ queries are necessary for seven or more agents, even when valuations are additive. Thus, we resolve the five-agent case and, more broadly, determine whether polylogarithmic query complexity is possible for every number of agents except six. We also explore the computational complexity of finding contiguous $\varepsilon$-envy-free allocations. When monotone Lipschitz valuations are given by polynomial-time evaluation procedures (e.g., arithmetic circuits and efficiently computable Turing machines), we show that an $\varepsilon$-envy-free division can be computed in polynomial time for five agents. In contrast, even for additive valuations, finding an $\varepsilon$-envy-free division is UEOPL-hard for every fixed number of agents $n\ge7$ and PPAD-complete for every fixed $n\ge13$.

item.title: Affine Combiners for Reed-Solomon Proximity Gaps
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Chiesa, Guy Weissenberg, Eylon Yogev, Kai Zhe Zheng
item.description:
Main Reed–Solomon affine-combiner proximity gap theorem was formalized in Lean with AI assistance; Reed–Muller and equal-degree extensions are not covered.
Reed-Solomon proximity gaps establish soundness guarantees for protocols that test received words through random combinations. For length-$n$ codes over $\mathbb{F}_q$, classical scalar combiners achieve error $O(n/q)$ in the unique-decoding regime, with larger known bounds near the Johnson radius. We prove smaller error bounds using affine combiners, which combine two received words $f,g$ as $f(x)+(α+βx)g(x)$, where $α,β$ are independent uniform elements of $\mathbb{F}_q$. For output degree bound $d=ρn$, fixed $ρ\in(0,1)$ and $0<η<1-\sqrtρ$, and sufficiently large block length $n$, we prove mutual correlated agreement (MCA) with one coordinate of agreement loss at threshold $A=\lceil(\sqrtρ+η)n\rceil$, with error $O_{ρ,η}\left(\frac{1}{q}+\frac{n^2}{q^2}\right)$. The result holds over arbitrary evaluation domains in every finite field, including prime and binary extension fields. The agreement threshold can approach the Johnson threshold, beyond unique decoding. For $q\ge n^2$, our error is $O_{ρ,η}(1/q)$, an asymptotic factor-$n$ separation from scalar combiners: we prove that their worst-case MCA error is $Ω_{ρ,η}(n/q)$ at the same agreement threshold and with the same one-coordinate loss. We also prove that affine combiners incur worst-case error $Ω_{ρ,η}(n/q)$ when no agreement loss is allowed. Thus one coordinate of agreement loss is necessary for our guarantee; this relaxation of standard MCA reduces the guaranteed common agreement fraction by at most $1/n$. We also extend the result to $k$-variate Reed-Muller codes on subfield grids, obtaining MCA error $O_{ρ,η,k}(q^{-k})$ for fixed $ρ,η,k$, sufficiently large $n$, and $q\ge n^{k+1}$, with agreement loss $n^{1-1/k}$.

item.title: Do Embedding-Map Distances Guide LLM Ideation? Four Tests Against What Came Next
item.dc:creator: Javier Aguilar Martín
item.description:
Three impossibility results about decoding embedding-space targets into coherent text (e.g., two_worlds) are machine-checked in Lean 4 in the paper's repository.
A popular ideation recipe treats an embedding map of existing work as a guide: pick points far from everything and decode them into ideas. I test four ways such distances could guide ideation against what appeared later. (1) Far random directions are not text: no later item reaches a raw cosine above about 0.10 with one (after centring or whitening, 22 of 24 cells stay out of reach), and an LLM decoder shown a target's neighbours, with score-only feedback, writes those neighbours in all six target sets. A neighbour-free search writes coherent text at median cosine 0.57 and 0.47 to interior gaps, beating the nearest existing item on 15 and 14 of 20, but only 0.07 and 0.06 to far points. (2) On k-means cells of a past-only map, the registered hole score mostly tracks cell size and position; three density-based gap scores forecast which cells grow fastest at or below chance (AUC 0.30 to 0.66) and add nothing to momentum in Steam and arXiv, with patents inconclusive; more isolated new Steam games are slightly better reviewed. (3) LLM continuations of arXiv papers stay closer to the source than papers that cite it, under three user prompts and against proposal rewrites (gpt-4o) and April-December 2023 papers (OLMo). Critique lengthens this step beyond content-free revision, replicated on 150 new papers. Revealing a real follow-up's title turns the ideas by 0.032 along a follow-up-specific direction beyond revision; reviewer, oracle and distance feedback add 0.13, 0.08 and 0.34 of that turn (upper bounds 0.46, 0.46, 0.70), and their turn is not separable from revision or their longer step. (4) For inspiration material graded by distance, no inverted U was detected, on an anticipation margin that tracks format more than content. Original tests were registered before running, follow-ups (thirteen requested in two AI-agent reviews) after the main results; all are dated only by local git commits.

item.title: An Adaptive Reduced Speed of Light Approximation
item.dc:creator: Chong-Chong He, Mark R. Krumholz, Benjamin D. Wibking
item.description:
Stability-bound proofs from the von Neumann analysis, including the unequal-opacity extension and appendix lemmas, are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib.
The reduced speed of light approximation (RSLA) is a common approach in radiation-hydrodynamic (RHD) simulations of non-relativistic systems where the gas speed $v_{\rm gas} \ll c$. In the RSLA one eases the severe time step constraint imposed by the speed of light $c$ by replacing it with a reduced value $\hat{c}$ chosen so that $v_{\rm gas} \ll \hat{c} \ll c$. This approach works well in flows with low or moderate optical depth, but fails in optically thick media, where it makes thermal relaxation too slow and gives incorrect RHD wave modes. Here we propose an Adaptive Reduced Speed of Light Approximation (ARSA) that removes these problems by replacing the global speed reduction factor $φ_0 \equiv \hat{c}/c$ with a local, cell-by-cell reduction factor $φ$ derived from a von Neumann stability analysis of the implicit-explicit update used by modern two-moment RHD codes. The resulting limiter has no tunable parameters, can be computed using only local operations, and improves on the classic RSLA by allowing $φ\to 1$ in cells where a reduced speed of light is not required because the exchange with the gas damps unstable modes, allowing recovery of the correct thermal relaxation and wave-damping rates in highly-opaque regions. We compare ARSA to the classic RSLA in a range of standard RHD test problems, and show that in opaque regions where gas holds most of the heat capacity the ARSA is much more accurate than the RSLA at the same time step, or that it can achieve the same accuracy as the RSLA with up to 100 times fewer time steps. However, gains are limited in regions where radiation holds a large share of the heat capacity, as it does in some astrophysical systems.

item.title: Turing Agent: Agentic Formal Verification for Mathematical Research
item.dc:creator: Yang Chen, Qianyi Wang, Ronghui Yang, Zhanhao Li, Yu Cong, Chen Zhang, Hangfan Zhang, Shao Zhang, Shuai Li, Toru Takisaka, Chao Xu, Yi Zhou, Zhihao Tang, Xiao Wang, Bo Zhang, Shuyue Hu
item.description:
LLM agent harness that formalizes research-level TCS theorem statements and proofs in Lean using Mathlib and CSLib, checked by Lean's kernel.
Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing mathematical discovery, moving beyond benchmark-level problem solving to tackle frontier research problems. This progress is ushering mathematics into an era of proof abundance, raising a fundamental challenge: how can we ensure the correctness of the ever-growing volume of AI-generated proofs and transform them into trustworthy, machine-verified mathematical knowledge? We introduce Turing Agent, an agent harness designed to orchestrate end-to-end formal verification of research-level mathematics. Its wo-scale architecture integrates theorem formalization and proof formalization agents, empowered by structured proof decomposition, parallel verification, accumulated proof experience, and selective semantic review. Leveraging our collaborations with theoretical computer science (TCS) researchers, we focus our evaluation on TCS, a particularly demanding domain characterized by intricate quantification, complex dependencies, and stringent semantic requirements. Against direct generation and general-purpose coding harnesses, including Codex CLI and Claude Code, Turing Agent achieves approximately 57-62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% overall pass@1 on a TCS-focused subset of RLMEval, using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Notably, Turing Agent, built on DeepSeek, successfully completes the formal verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks from OpenAI's October 2026 collection. One particularly challenging TCS problem required about a hundred formally verified auxiliary claims. Moreover, by actively exploring and refining the formalization process, Turing Agent can uncover simpler alternative proofs, expose unnecessary dependencies in original proofs, and generate reusable mathematical knowledge as a byproduct of verification.

item.title: GPRidge: Gaussian-process Accelerated Calculations of Minimum Energy Paths and First-order Saddle Points
item.dc:creator: Rohit Goswami, Maxim Masterov, Satish Kamath, Alejandro Pena-Torres, Andreas Lynge Vishart, Thomas Bligaard, Hannes Jonsson
item.description:
A supplementary Lean 4 development formalizes some of the paper's labelled theorems: squared-exponential kernel identities, a Schur comparison, local stability of the reflected mode, and gradient-error bounds.
GPRidge, a Gaussian-process (GP) library for accelerating calculations of minimum energy paths and first-order saddle points with compiled-language and Python bindings, is presented. An evaluation controller uses GP predictions to iteratively adjust the Cartesian coordinates of the atoms. The fitted GP energy surface and measured energies and forces pass from the path calculation to local refinement of the saddle point. New evaluations improve the surrogate and check the candidate geometry. For the molecular calculations, acceptance requires measured-force convergence and an independent Hessian with only one negative eigenvalue. A second negative eigenvalue triggers an escape and renewed refinement. The controller supports a joint inverse-distance GP for molecules and local GP residuals on periodic systems. Applications to the 24 Baker-Chan and 20 Birkholz-Schlegel molecular reactions using the Universal Model for Atoms (UMA-S-1.1), and to 72 Pt heptamer and island rearrangements on Pt(111) using a Morse potential, are presented. On matched Baker-Chan reactions, GPRidge uses 7.8- and 7.0-fold fewer energy-and-force evaluations than climbing-image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) and off-path climbing-image nudged elastic band (OCI-NEB), respectively, reducing validation-inclusive CI-NEB time by 41%. All 20 Birkholz-Schlegel saddle points pass the independent index-one check, compared with 17 for the classical dimer method started from the same path maxima; on those 17 reactions, the GP dimer stage uses 6.4-fold fewer evaluations. All 72 Pt(111) paths meet the OptBench force criterion, with median evaluation counts of 30 and 23 for the heptamer and island problems, against 778 and 443 for CI-NEB.

item.title: Centered Ablation: Why Last-Layer Directional Ablation Under-Fires or Collapses, and a Closed-Form Fix
item.dc:creator: Quy-Anh Dang, Chris Ngo
item.description:
The proofs of the closed-form ablation results were formalized and machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with assistant help.
Directional ablation removes a hidden state's component along a "behaviour direction" while a language model runs. It is the standard way to switch a behaviour such as refusal off, but it is erratic: on some models it barely fires, on others the text collapses into repetition. We show why, and fix it. At the last residual stream, ablation is exactly a logit bias: a fixed vocabulary footprint scaled by a gate, the cosine between the hidden state and the direction. The gate is measured from the origin, but last-layer states share a large common mode far from it, so a direction that overlaps the common mode fires on benign text and under-fires on its targets. Centered Ablation (CA) projects the common mode out of the direction, in closed form. Across 8 models, CA raises attack success by 29 and 46 points where the standard recipe under-fires, cuts collapse on Gemma-2-9B from 50% to 1%, and preserves 12 to 40 points more benign answers on high-overlap models, 39 to 46 more than the affine offset of prior work. Two numbers computed before generation predict, on models the analysis had not seen, which gain faithfulness and which gain attack success, and a collapse index marks when text degenerates. We also show that two standard safety judges score collapsed text in opposite directions, which can fabricate a 46-point effect.

item.title: A Solution to the Birkhoff Problem
item.dc:creator: Kevin Schlegel
item.description:
Matrix-equation computations reducing the classification were carried out by an AI model and formally verified in Lean 4 using Mathlib.
For a commutative uniserial ring $R$ of length $n$ we describe the indecomposable objects in the monomorphism category of $R$ independent of the specific ring for $n\leq 5$ and only dependent on the residue field for $n = 6$. Thus, the classification problem for the monomorphism category of $\mathbb{Z}/p^6 \mathbb{Z}$ reduces to the known case of $\mathbb{F}_p[x]/(x^6)$, resolving the Birkhoff Problem.

item.title: Veech dichotomy for specific covering surface over Veech surface
item.dc:creator: Haoran Hu
item.description:
The main theorem (Theorem 1, compact branch configurations implying unique ergodicity of minimal directions) is formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, provided in a code repository.
It is known that Veech dichotomy, which states that minimal directions are uniquely ergodic, holds for Veech surface and covering surface branched at a single non-periodic connection point of Veech surface. We give a sufficient condition for Veech dichotomy holds for a finite translation cover of a Veech surface, and applies it on branched cover of square-tiled surfaces to construct examples that satisfy Veech dichotomy but aren't Veech surfaces.

item.title: Composable Rewrites for Layouts of Algebraic Data Types
item.dc:creator: Christophe Gyurgyik, Alexander J Root, Benjamin Driscoll, Gabriel Radanne, Fredrik Kjolstad, Clément Pit-Claudel
item.description:
The layout language, rewrite rules, local refinement criterion, soundness and storage-recovery theorems are mechanized in Lean, with each formal statement cross-referenced to a Lean declaration.
Algebraic data types (ADTs) decouple the logical structure of data from physical layout choices that affect performance. For example, packing small fields into a word improves spatial locality, while storing co-accessed fields contiguously can enable vectorization. Such choices reinforce or undermine one another, with ramifications for compiler optimizations and memory management. Their interplay creates a combinatorial space of layouts with different runtime costs and memory footprints. The most favorable layout depends on the program's construction and destruction patterns, the characteristics of input data, and the target machine. Exploring this space requires control over layout decisions and a way to compose them while preserving program semantics. We provide both through rewrite rules over layouts, independent of any particular source language or bit-level encoding. Starting from a canonical layout derived from the ADT, these rules transform its representation while leaving the source program intact. We identify a local refinement criterion for proving each rewrite rule correct, so that layouts continue to represent every value and keep distinct values apart. Adding a new rule therefore only requires a proof satisfying this local criterion. We realize these rules in Isomer, a new pure functional programming language whose compiler specializes construction, pattern matching, and memory management to the chosen layouts. Using a default layout for all ADTs, Isomer achieves competitive performance against established functional compilers that automatically select layouts. Our rewrites further improve performance by tailoring layouts to each workload, permitting representations that prior work cannot attain or can only achieve through explicit changes to the source code.

item.title: Spread Too Thin: How Higher Resolution Dilutes a Vision Transformer's Attention, and a Training-Free Rescaling
item.dc:creator: Neil D. B. Bruce
item.description:
Every mathematical statement about softmax attention dilution and the log-ratio rescaling is proved in Lean 4 and released as ancillary files.
A vision transformer read at a higher resolution than it was trained at spreads each attention row over many more patches, yet every row must still hand out exactly one unit of weight.
